content: The requirements for facilities, equipment, and supplies for the placement and removal of male circumcision (MC) devices depend on the type of device being used. For collar clamp devices, the necessary facilities and equipment are similar to those required for conventional surgical male circumcision. Although sutures are not typically needed for hemostasis, a sterile field, sterile instruments, injectable anesthesia, and immediate on-site surgical backup are essential. This is particularly important in case the device slips after the foreskin is cut, leading to loss of hemostasis and requiring intervention to control bleeding and close the wound. In studies involving elastic collar compression devices, sterile settings or instruments were not required for placement; clean examination gloves were sufficient. However, sterile instruments were necessary for removal, which was considered a clean procedure and performed in the same type of facilities as placement. These device procedures do not require injectable anesthesia or sutures. However, if the device displaces, is removed prematurely, or complications arise during foreskin removal, surgical intervention with appropriate equipment, including local injectable anesthesia and suturing, may be necessary. All sites offering these procedures must be prepared to manage such events appropriately. For collar clamp devices, immediate on-site surgical supplies are required at the time of placement. For elastic collar compression devices, surgical resources must be available within 6–12 hours in case of device displacement or removal during the week the device is worn. Additionally, appropriate accessory equipment and supplies, as well as emergency equipment for methods requiring injectable anesthesia, must be available. Pain management medications should be provided during and after device placement, throughout the week the device is worn, and at removal, following standard protocols. Clinical safety and efficacy studies have shown that a team of two trained providers is typically required for device placement—one acting as the operator and the other as an assistant. The number of providers needed for device removal is less clear, with some studies suggesting one and others two. Until more data is available, it is prudent to have a second provider assist with device removal, especially for elastic collar compression devices. Providers in these studies included physicians, clinical officers, and nurses, all of whom were deemed competent and performed device placement and removal safely. Compared to conventional surgical methods, device-assisted circumcision is simpler and does not require routine suturing skills. However, skills in working within a sterile field and administering injectable anesthesia are necessary for collar clamp devices. Surgical services remain essential for men under 18 years of age, those ineligible for device methods, or clients who prefer surgical circumcision. Although devices are designed to remain in place during routine daily activities, instances of device slippage (with collar clamp devices) or displacement (with elastic collar compression devices) have been reported. Such events may require surgical intervention to prevent serious complications. While these events occurred in approximately 5% of subjects in studies, their frequency in routine healthcare settings is not yet determined. Therefore, while the person performing the circumcision does not need surgical skills, an experienced and qualified clinician must be available on-site or at a referral center, depending on the device type. These clinicians should have specialized skills to manage complications such as retracted vessels (for collar clamp devices) or abnormal foreskin anatomy (for elastic ring compression devices), as swelling and blistering can distort penile anatomy. Healthcare providers must recognize the limits of their skills and know the appropriate steps to take if complications occur. When using a device method, a second visit is required for device removal, and services must be organized to accommodate both visits at a one-week interval. Although studies indicated that collar clamp devices could detach spontaneously without significant consequences, men often preferred removal by a provider due to discomfort or pain associated with spontaneous detachment. Medical male circumcision (MMC) is part of a comprehensive HIV prevention strategy and does not provide complete protection against HIV. It complements, rather than replaces, other prevention strategies. The WHO-recommended minimum package for male circumcision includes information on the risks and benefits of the procedure, counseling on safer sexual practices, access to HIV testing, condom promotion and provision, and management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). MMC, whether performed surgically or using devices, should always be integrated into a broader HIV prevention strategy, ensuring clients receive all elements of the package. Informed consent is a critical component of MMC. It is the voluntary agreement of an individual to undergo circumcision, regardless of the method used. All site staff must be trained in the principles of informed consent and the appropriate methods to obtain it. Adult men seeking MMC have the right to receive full information on the benefits and risks of circumcision and the specific method or device to be used. Men should be provided with accurate information to help them decide whether a device method is the best option for them and to commit to the conditions of use. Client education and counseling are essential, even though device-assisted circumcision takes less time than conventional surgery. Opportunities for education and counseling include HIV counseling and testing before device placement, at the time of placement, and during the second visit for device removal. The return visit also provides an opportunity for further education and HIV prevention counseling. It is important to determine if a man is a good candidate for device use, considering factors such as travel during the week the device is worn and availability for the follow-up visit. Men who are not eligible for a device method should be informed about the option of conventional surgical circumcision. Specific instructions and educational messages will vary with each device, but in general, it is important to emphasize the need for the device to remain in place for a week, avoid activities that might displace the device (including sexual intercourse and masturbation), and seek prompt follow-up if displacement occurs. Clients should also be discouraged from self-removal of the device and clearly informed about the need to return for a second visit for device removal by a trained provider. Additionally, they should abstain from sexual activity or consistently use condoms for 6–7 weeks after device removal until the wound is fully healed. Manufacturer instructions for device use are not sufficient for competent performance. Device-specific clinical guidelines should be developed, including protocols for placement and removal, recognition and management of complications, and referral protocols for clients ineligible for device methods. Training is essential for all medical MMC providers. Device-assisted circumcision outcomes performed by well-trained clinical officers or nurses are comparable to those of surgical circumcision performed by trained surgeons. Training courses for device use do not need to teach surgical skills but must thoroughly educate providers on the risks of device slippage, displacement, or self-removal, and how to manage such cases. Providers should know which specialty centers or clinicians to contact for appropriate intervention within the recommended timeframe. Supervision systems should support trained providers to perform MMC safely and maintain competence. Quality assurance standards for MMC services remain relevant but may need revision to accommodate device use. These standards include effective management systems, provision of the WHO minimum package of services, availability of necessary medicines and equipment, and training of qualified providers. Service delivery modes, including fixed, mobile, and outreach sites, should be adapted to meet the requirements for device use, ensuring surgical backup is available when needed. Community awareness and demand creation are important for the successful introduction of MMC devices. Accurate information about devices, their benefits, and risks should be provided, and misconceptions addressed. The community should be informed that MMC services are voluntary, high-quality, and safe, with trained providers using WHO-prequalified devices. Program planners must assess and plan for the costs, logistics, and waste management requirements of introducing devices. Monitoring consumption at the site level is essential for accurate forecasting and timely procurement.
